records.title: Touch of evil: the terrifying truth about sleep paralysis
records.summary: One in five people have experienced this frightening state – and the Harvard neuroscientist Baland Jalal has dedicated his career to studying it. Could it be a portal to a deeper understanding of the mind? The Harvard neuroscientist Baland Jalal is considering the unfathomable depths of the human brain. “It can contemplate itself, and vast galaxies, spirits, souls, poetry, Einstein. Yet you hold it in your hand and it seems so trivial.” Jalal’s passion – the subject that drove him to become a scientist – is sleep paralysis, a brain glitch that can fill its host with terror so palpable that it can cause lasting trauma. “What you get very close to in sleep paralysis,” he says, “is that subjective world of the mind. It’s very hard to put into words.” He should know – he’s spent 271 pages trying to do so. His new book, The Phantom Mind, argues that by exploring the borderlands of sleep, where sleep paralysis occurs, we can delve deeper into how all aspects of our minds work. records.title: Hegseth dodges impeachment after using troops and vets for cover
records.summary: Observers are reporting that absent Democrats likely torpedoed Thomas Massie's attempt to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth in the House last night. The vote to refer his eight articles of impeachment to the judiciary committee for a sure death, passed 211-204. Hegseth and his compadres in the Pentagon are no doubt feeling vindicated since he spent Tuesday morning boasting of his handling of the war policies in Yemen, the Caribbean, Venezuela, and in particular, Iran. In order to do this he had to engage in some serious fabrications about the state of the war: that it was "won," that Iran's military is "in ruin," the "ironclad blockade (is) unbroken," that "we control the Strait of Hormuz." It is worth watching in full . "For the first time in American history, a cabinet secretary overseeing America's military is being attacked not for losing conflicts with our enemies, but for winning them," Hegseth declared. records.title: ‘The cold is lethal’: storms leave thousands in Gaza without shelter
records.summary: Charities warn of lack of protection amid health fears for more than 940,000 displaced people living in flood-prone areas Tens of thousands of Palestinians have been left in waterlogged and damaged tents after deadly storms at the weekend, while 150,000 new shelters are held outside Gaza awaiting Israeli approval to enter, aid agencies have said. At least four Palestinian children and woman were killed as heavy rains and wind battered fragile, leaky tents. Thousands have been left without shelter and sanitation infrastructure has been destroyed, with sewage spewing into people’s tents. Continue reading...

records.title: AIPAC dumped more than $55 million into losing midterm races
records.summary: The largest pro-Israel group in the U.S., the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), has been silent on social media since Tuesday afternoon, well before polls closed across the country and Democrats won both chambers of Congress in a blue wave, largely driven by dissatisfaction over rising costs sparked by the war in Iran. The group was an early supporter of the war and a major funder of ads attacking House and Senate candidates calling to cut off aid to Israel. It spent big on the 2026 midterm elections, dumping $84.1 million via its super PAC, United Democracy Project (UDP), and several other PACs into races that have been decided as of this writing. AIPAC might be silent today because they need to explain to their donors how nearly-two-thirds, or $55.3 million, of that spending went to races in which the group’s preferred candidate lost. A failure to achieve the desired results from two-thirds of its political spending will be a tough reality to present to donors, especially when AIPAC repeatedly claims that “being pro-Israel is good policy and good politics.” AIPAC’s failures to deliver results for its donors stands in sharp contrast with the 2022 midterm election,

records.title: Major losses could spur Trump to escalate war before year's end
records.summary: As much as the Iran war is the key reason Trump and the GOP were crushed tonight, it is important to recognize that the pressure for war is now likely to increase . This does not mean that Trump will restart the war. But the balance of pressure for and against war will likely favor escalation. Trump was under a degree of pressure to strike a deal before the midterms, hoping to soften the blow in the polls. But now that the midterms are over, that pressure will dissipate somewhat. Gas prices are still high, but the political cost has already been paid. There won’t be another point on the political calendar for some time when that cost can be exacted again. But two other factors will intensify. First, pro-war elements in Israel and in Washington will see the next two months as the last period in which Trump has wide maneuverability to restart the war. By January, the Democrats will control both chambers, will control the purse, and can begin impeaching Trump’s secretaries, including Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. records.summary: Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) announced Tuesday that they would not back Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) in his effort to become majority leader next year. The duo — leading voices on the center and left of the Democratic Party — took pains to avoid discussing specific policy issues, arguing instead that it is time for a new generation of leaders to take charge. "If this campaign was about anything, it was about change," Sanders said, adding that “poll after poll suggests that the American people want bold change.” “The public is done with people who say a lot of words but aren’t actually going to put more money in people’s pockets,” Slotkin said. “I personally will work with anyone who wants to work on that mission instead of looking like we’re doing things.” Neither Sanders nor Slotkin specified who they would support in the race for majority leader, though Slotkin said she had a “productive conversation” with Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Mary.) about his potential candidacy. The joint press conference suggests that momentum is building behind the effort to find new Democratic leadership in the Senate. records.title: How years of research built Grand Theft Auto VI’s obsessively detailed world
records.summary: The developers behind its virtual Florida share how they built their most ambitious world so far • Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here In 2015, a group of Grand Theft Auto developers from Rockstar North took their first trips to Miami to do field research for the next game in the phenomenally popular crime series. “Before you’re doing hyper-organised research trips, you’re immersing yourself in the place and its history, the vibe of it,” Rob Nelson, one of the lead developers on GTA VI, tells me. “[You see] the physical places you want to move characters through, the experiences you want them to have, and the juxtaposition between the extremes of society that are in Miami.” I wondered: did people ever recognise them on any of their research trips? Did locals know what they were doing? This is the biggest game in the world, after all; I imagine it would be difficult to go entirely undercover. “We’re always semi-undercover,” he says. “But if you have a bunch of dorks going through a terrifying neighbourhood, you do stick out a bit.” Continue reading...

records.title: 9/11 vets: Do politicians take the decision to go to war seriously?
records.summary: It is Veterans Day again, which means that, alongside the free red, white, and blue pancake specials and complimentary coffees, Americans will post tributes honoring the ultimate sacrifice of our soldiers. Just as predictably, on Memorial Day, veterans will receive well-intentioned messages thanking them for their service. Of course, Memorial Day honors those who died while serving in the U.S. military, whereas Veterans Day recognizes all who have served. This confusion is hardly something to get worked up about in itself. But it is symptomatic of something more consequential: a nation detached from its military and the wars it fights. In a sense, Americans are not wrong to conflate the two holidays. Service and sacrifice cannot be neatly separated, especially when the military has become an instrument of statecraft, diplomacy, humanitarian assistance, and lethal force whose deployment increasingly depends less on congressional authorization than on the decisions of a single president. Less than 1% of Americans serve in the military. records.title: Vance admits it: ‘The reason we lost is the war’
records.summary: Wednesday morning, as Democrats celebrated one of the largest midterm blowouts in decades, Vice President J.D. Vance struck a somber tone. “The reason we lost is the war,” Vance wrote on X, referencing the Iran conflict the Trump administration launched in February of this year. “If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so,” he continued. “But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.” While Vance has long hinted at skepticism toward the Iran war, the comments represent an unusually clear criticism by a vice president of his own president’s policy. The statement suggests Vance sees a need to distance himself from the conflict in hopes of bolstering his future political fortunes, particularly ahead of a likely run for president in 2028. President Donald Trump acknowledged Tuesday that Iran “was a piece of it” but insisted that he “did the right thing. I would have done it again.” Indeed, there is little doubt that the Iran war played a decisive role in the Democrats’ dominant performance on Tuesday. records.title: After midterm disaster, can Rubio still get Cuba regime change?
records.summary: After Democrats dominated last week’s midterm elections, retaking control of the House and Senate, President Donald Trump has turned his attention southward. “Cuba is falling. It’s a failing nation. It’s got an ideology very similar to what the Democrat ideology is,” he said Monday. “I would imagine it will fall fairly soon.” The comments suggest that, despite facing a stunning rebuke of his foreign-policy adventurism in Iran, Trump is not quite ready to give up on his goal, reiterated as recently as last month, of overthrowing the Cuban government. So is Trump poised to go beyond economic pressure and saber rattling by launching a military campaign against Cuba? records.summary: Billionaire Nvidia founder Jensen Huang, who is currently holding the entire U.S. economy on his leather jacket-wearing back, has allegedly been canoodling with an AI executive-turned-Chinese spy. You might expect this news to terrify Silicon Valley, the home of the new age defense contractors. You might expect calls for Huang's head. Not exactly. “He did something incredibly dumb,” Shaun Maguire, an investor at Silicon Valley giant Sequoia Capital, posted on X . However, “I believe Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership.” Jason Calacanis of the All-In Podcast joined in. “Jensen and NVIDIA’s technology are a critical target, and we need to protect them both," he wrote . The tepid reaction shows a splintering of the tech-China hawk movement. Moguls in this space have spent the last few years spreading fear over China’s potential AI dominance — in part because of a belief in American exceptionalism, but also out of fierce self-interest. records.title: 9/11 vets: Do politicians take the decision to go to war seriously?
records.summary: It is Veterans Day again, which means that, alongside the free red, white, and blue pancake specials and complimentary coffees, Americans will post tributes honoring the ultimate sacrifice of our soldiers. Just as predictably, on Memorial Day, veterans will receive well-intentioned messages thanking them for their service. Of course, Memorial Day honors those who died while serving in the U.S. military, whereas Veterans Day recognizes all who have served. This confusion is hardly something to get worked up about in itself. But it is symptomatic of something more consequential: a nation detached from its military and the wars it fights. In a sense, Americans are not wrong to conflate the two holidays. Service and sacrifice cannot be neatly separated, especially when the military has become an instrument of statecraft, diplomacy, humanitarian assistance, and lethal force whose deployment increasingly depends less on congressional authorization than on the decisions of a single president. Less than 1% of Americans serve in the military. records.title: AIPAC dumped more than $55 million into losing midterm races
records.summary: The largest pro-Israel group in the U.S., the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), has been silent on social media since Tuesday afternoon, well before polls closed across the country and Democrats won both chambers of Congress in a blue wave, largely driven by dissatisfaction over rising costs sparked by the war in Iran. The group was an early supporter of the war and a major funder of ads attacking House and Senate candidates calling to cut off aid to Israel. It spent big on the 2026 midterm elections, dumping $84.1 million via its super PAC, United Democracy Project (UDP), and several other PACs into races that have been decided as of this writing. AIPAC might be silent today because they need to explain to their donors how nearly-two-thirds, or $55.3 million, of that spending went to races in which the group’s preferred candidate lost. A failure to achieve the desired results from two-thirds of its political spending will be a tough reality to present to donors, especially when AIPAC repeatedly claims that “being pro-Israel is good policy and good politics.” AIPAC’s failures to deliver results for its donors stands in sharp contrast with the 2022 midterm election,

records.title: Vance admits it: ‘The reason we lost is the war’
records.summary: Wednesday morning, as Democrats celebrated one of the largest midterm blowouts in decades, Vice President J.D. Vance struck a somber tone. “The reason we lost is the war,” Vance wrote on X, referencing the Iran conflict the Trump administration launched in February of this year. “If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so,” he continued. “But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.” While Vance has long hinted at skepticism toward the Iran war, the comments represent an unusually clear criticism by a vice president of his own president’s policy. The statement suggests Vance sees a need to distance himself from the conflict in hopes of bolstering his future political fortunes, particularly ahead of a likely run for president in 2028. President Donald Trump acknowledged Tuesday that Iran “was a piece of it” but insisted that he “did the right thing. I would have done it again.” Indeed, there is little doubt that the Iran war played a decisive role in the Democrats’ dominant performance on Tuesday. records.title: Major losses could spur Trump to escalate war before year's end
records.summary: As much as the Iran war is the key reason Trump and the GOP were crushed tonight, it is important to recognize that the pressure for war is now likely to increase . This does not mean that Trump will restart the war. But the balance of pressure for and against war will likely favor escalation. Trump was under a degree of pressure to strike a deal before the midterms, hoping to soften the blow in the polls. But now that the midterms are over, that pressure will dissipate somewhat. Gas prices are still high, but the political cost has already been paid. There won’t be another point on the political calendar for some time when that cost can be exacted again. But two other factors will intensify. First, pro-war elements in Israel and in Washington will see the next two months as the last period in which Trump has wide maneuverability to restart the war. By January, the Democrats will control both chambers, will control the purse, and can begin impeaching Trump’s secretaries, including Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. Chris Van Hollen (D-Mary.) about his potential candidacy. The joint press conference suggests that momentum is building behind the effort to find new Democratic leadership in the Senate. records.title: Are Democrats ready to make the most of the blue wave?
records.summary: Unless you’ve been living under a rock (no shame Patrick Star!), you’ve likely heard about last Tuesday’s “Blue Wave” midterm elections . The Democrats’ strong performance at the polls flipped control of the House and the Senate, delivering stunning results on the way, including flipping long-time red states like Kansas and Texas. As the GOP scrambles to repair the damage and Democrats strategize about how to use their new power in a divided Washington, one takeaway seems obvious: this was a foreign policy election, in which the Iran war and the costs it brought home served as the tipping point. But can we read these election results as a repudiation of U.S. foreign policy writ-large, or is this a specific response to one of the dumbest interventions in the long history of American adventurism? What does JD Vance's day-after effort to distance himself from the war tell us about how Republicans are digesting this result? And if Tuesday was a rebuke of U.S. foreign policy as usual, are Democrats ready to respond accordingly? records.title: After midterm disaster, can Rubio still get Cuba regime change?
records.summary: After Democrats dominated last week’s midterm elections, retaking control of the House and Senate, President Donald Trump has turned his attention southward. “Cuba is falling. It’s a failing nation. It’s got an ideology very similar to what the Democrat ideology is,” he said Monday. “I would imagine it will fall fairly soon.” The comments suggest that, despite facing a stunning rebuke of his foreign-policy adventurism in Iran, Trump is not quite ready to give up on his goal, reiterated as recently as last month, of overthrowing the Cuban government. So is Trump poised to go beyond economic pressure and saber rattling by launching a military campaign against Cuba? The answer is “no” — or at least “not yet.” Many analysts predict that a lame-duck president constrained by domestic setbacks could seek redemption through foreign-policy achievements, including by lashing out at seemingly easier targets like an impoverished Caribbean nation. records.title: Private renters in the UK: how difficult is the rental market where you live?
records.summary: We’d like to hear from private renters about rising costs, finding somewhere to live and dealing with landlords Private renters are facing steep rent rises and a shortage of affordable properties, with growing numbers of landlords selling up. The Renters’ Rights Act, which came into force in England in May, introduced new protections for tenants, but many continue to face uncertainty about their housing. While some renters have successfully secured reductions , others are struggling with soaring costs and a highly competitive rental market. Meanwhile England’s housing courts have been overloaded with renters battling evictions . Continue reading...

records.title: Major losses could spur Trump to escalate war before year's end
records.summary: As much as the Iran war is the key reason Trump and the GOP were crushed tonight, it is important to recognize that the pressure for war is now likely to increase . This does not mean that Trump will restart the war. But the balance of pressure for and against war will likely favor escalation. Trump was under a degree of pressure to strike a deal before the midterms, hoping to soften the blow in the polls. But now that the midterms are over, that pressure will dissipate somewhat. Gas prices are still high, but the political cost has already been paid. There won’t be another point on the political calendar for some time when that cost can be exacted again. But two other factors will intensify. First, pro-war elements in Israel and in Washington will see the next two months as the last period in which Trump has wide maneuverability to restart the war. By January, the Democrats will control both chambers, will control the purse, and can begin impeaching Trump’s secretaries, including Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. records.title: Scorned Trump boots Rwanda, South Africa from trade deal
records.summary: Last week, the Trump administration announced that, beginning January 1, South Africa and Rwanda will stop receiving preferential trade access to the U.S. market through the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA). This decision comes down to issues that have little to do with the act itself, nor even really with trade between the United States and these countries. Rather, in both cases, their removal from AGOA serves as an act of retribution from a president unhappy with their governments’ policies on domestic or regional issues. But American interests themselves will suffer, as consumers will be forced to pay higher prices for the same goods. The preferential trade agreement — originally signed into law in 2000 by President Bill Clinton and most recently renewed in September for two additional years — provides duty-free access for over 7,000 goods to the U.S. market for qualifying sub-Saharan countries. In exchange for this preferential access, AGOA requires countries to meet a set of vague requirements, including reducing barriers to American exporters, ensuring governance and human rights standards, and not posing a threat to U.S. national security and foreign policy interest

records.title: Paraguay's Trump-aligned president resigns amid bank crisis
records.summary: After being feted around Washington a mere two weeks ago, Paraguayan President Santiago Peña resigned Thursday amid ongoing impeachment proceedings over his irregular ties to a top digital bank that collapsed this week, locking out nearly half of the South American country’s population from its savings and pensions. The scandal over the now-insolvent ueno bank, which holds $850m in public funds and serves nearly 3 million customers, accelerated this week with the resignation of the country’s central bank president, former ueno executive Carlos Carvalho, as scrutiny mounted over its loans to individuals connected to Peña, who held a large stake in the bank’s parent company, Grupo Vásquez, until last year. The escalating political scandal rattles a quickly-growing economy nestled between Argentina and Brazil that has attracted foreign investors and significant Trump administration attention because of its immense hydropower resources for operating data centers; close ties to Israel and Taiwan; and eagerness to expand security cooperation with the U.S. Peña, a Trump ally and conservative economist, had for months dismissed scrutiny of ueno’s finances and conflicts of interest. records.title: Neocons in full meltdown as voters punish GOP for Iran war
records.summary: It has long been claimed that Americans do not vote based on foreign policy, but the results of Tuesday’s midterm elections demonstrated the limits of this truism, with a large majority of voters rejecting the Iran War waged by the Trump administration. Even before the election, an October Fox News poll indicated that the Iran war and issues associated with it (inflation and gas prices) were among the top issues voters were concerned about. Exit polling published by NBC News showed 74% of voters saw the Iran war as a “crucial” or “major factor” in their vote, while 62% believed using force against Iran was the wrong decision. This apparently has come as a nasty surprise to the war’s biggest defenders and surrogates, who had assured their followers that this backlash would not happen. Some have admitted their errors, but many have not, and that split has rapidly produced a circular firing squad, with neocons aggressively turning on those in their ranks who have conceded the war was a mistake. records.title: 2026 wasn't the first time war swayed an election
records.summary: If foreign policy could decide an election, then 1992 upended expectations. Barely eight months after the Soviet flag was lowered from the Kremlin for the last time, President George H. W. Bush found himself reminding Americans that he had led the USSR peacefully into history’s dustbin while also liberating Kuwait from the clutches of Saddam Hussein. “My opponents say I spend too much time on foreign policy, as if it didn't matter that schoolchildren once hid under their desks in drills to prepare for nuclear war,” said Bush during his acceptance speech at the 1992 Republican National Convention. “Over the past 4 years, more people have breathed the fresh air of freedom than in all of human history.” Foreign policy mattered to Bush. He was a combat pilot during the Second World War and later served as ambassador to the United Nations, CIA Director, and Ronald Reagan’s vice president. It mattered a lot less to voters angry about a sluggish economy and high unemployment: 73% said the country was on the wrong track in 1992. records.title: Your Shopping Bag Runs Through Hormuz
records.summary: Your Shopping Bag Runs Through Hormuz Authored by Larry C. Johnson via Sonar21 , Every morning the cable networks put up the price of Brent and a graphic of a tanker, and every evening the experts reassure us that the oil is still flowing, more or less. Crude is the scoreboard everyone watches. It is also the wrong scoreboard. Iran has hit roughly fifty ships in and around the Strait of Hormuz since September 1, most of them tankers. Against a world fleet of more than 8,000 tankers, that is a rounding error. Washington's reassurance machine will tell you exactly that. What it won't tell you is that a good share of what moves through the strait isn't crude at all . It's the stuff the modern economy is actually made of: the feedstocks for plastics, the methanol for chemicals, the urea and ammonia for fertilizer. And those markets are far less forgiving than oil. If you want to know what Iran's tanker campaign really costs, stop looking at the gas pump. Look in your kitchen. What actually comes out of the Gulf Start with plastic. When I took a deep sniff, however, disaster: all I could smell was fertiliser! Instant coffee is brewed at scorching temperatures, then either freeze-dried in a vacuum or spray-dried using hot air. This industrial process strips away many of the volatile flavour compounds and bright aromas that make fresh coffee smell so good. records.summary: The humanitarian ceasefire in Oleshky, Ukraine, mediated by First Lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo XIV and jointly implemented by Ukraine and Russia, is unprecedented since the start of this war in 2022. Its success and people-centered spirit also stand in conspicuous contrast to the repeated attempts by the Trump administration to end the war, which have all ended in frustrated failure. There has been pragmatic, if intermittent, engagement between Russia and Ukraine virtually since the 2022 Russian invasion, around issues like the exchange of prisoners of war and the bodies of the fallen, or the Black Sea Grain Initiative . But until October 27, 2026, no humanitarian ceasefire along the frontline had ever been successfully implemented; it had never even been attempted. To facilitate these works, a temporary one-way traffic system will be in operation. During this period, north bound traffic will be permitted to travel from the Greenan Road junction along the Old Warrenpoint Road towards Greenbank Roundabout. Traffic travelling southbound should use the A2 Warrenpoint dual carriageway and turn left back into the Old Warrenpoint Road at Forest Hills. The one-way system will be in operation from 8:00am on Monday 12th October to 18:00pm Sunday 08th November 2026 and will remain in place continuously between these dates.

records.title: NI Water Works - Cornagrade Road Enniskillen 3 Aug
records.summary: Essential Water Infrastructure Improvement Work gets underway – Cornagrade Road, Enniskillen NI Water is set to commence an upgrade of the water infrastructure on Cornagrade Road, Enniskillen in early August for approximately 6 weeks. The work will see around 400m of new watermain being laid along Cornagrade Road, starting at Cherrymount Roundabout on Monday 3 rd August and progressing as far as the second entrance to Kilmacormick Road. To facilitate the laying of this new watermain, a lane closure will be in place around each working area and signage will be in place. Working areas will be kept as short as possible (around 100m) with temporary traffic lights in place to manage the flow of traffic. Access to residential and business properties on and adjacent to Cornagrade Road will be available at all times, although parking spaces within the working area will be affected for a short period of time while the pipelaying passes. Any bus stop located within a working area will be temporarily relocated.

records.title: Derry - NIW Scheme - Racecourse Rd - from 27 July
records.summary: Essential water network upgrade to get underway on Racecourse Road, Ballyarnett NI Water is set to begin an essential watermain upgrade on Racecourse Road, Ballyarnett (Derry/Londonderry) on Monday 27 th July to improve the resilience of the local water supply network. The work, which involves laying around 170 metres of new watermain between Carnhill Roundabout and Greenhaw Road, will replace a section of the 50-year-old Ballyarnett Water Trunkmain which has been prone to bursts. The upgrade will help to protect homes from flooding, should a burst occur in the future, and provide improved access for NI Water maintenance. A l ane closure controlled by temporary traffic lights will be in place on Racecourse Road around the working area from Monday 27 th July for four weeks. A further two weeks of work will take place in the adjacent verge which will not require any traffic management. Temporary traffic lights will be manned during peak hours and access to properties will be maintained at all times, although parking spaces within the working area will be temporarily unavailable. records.title: 9/11 vets: Do politicians take the decision to go to war seriously?
records.summary: It is Veterans Day again, which means that, alongside the free red, white, and blue pancake specials and complimentary coffees, Americans will post tributes honoring the ultimate sacrifice of our soldiers. Just as predictably, on Memorial Day, veterans will receive well-intentioned messages thanking them for their service. Of course, Memorial Day honors those who died while serving in the U.S. military, whereas Veterans Day recognizes all who have served. This confusion is hardly something to get worked up about in itself. But it is symptomatic of something more consequential: a nation detached from its military and the wars it fights. In a sense, Americans are not wrong to conflate the two holidays. Service and sacrifice cannot be neatly separated, especially when the military has become an instrument of statecraft, diplomacy, humanitarian assistance, and lethal force whose deployment increasingly depends less on congressional authorization than on the decisions of a single president. Less than 1% of Americans serve in the military. records.title: AIPAC dumped more than $55 million into losing midterm races
records.summary: The largest pro-Israel group in the U.S., the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), has been silent on social media since Tuesday afternoon, well before polls closed across the country and Democrats won both chambers of Congress in a blue wave, largely driven by dissatisfaction over rising costs sparked by the war in Iran. The group was an early supporter of the war and a major funder of ads attacking House and Senate candidates calling to cut off aid to Israel. It spent big on the 2026 midterm elections, dumping $84.1 million via its super PAC, United Democracy Project (UDP), and several other PACs into races that have been decided as of this writing. AIPAC might be silent today because they need to explain to their donors how nearly-two-thirds, or $55.3 million, of that spending went to races in which the group’s preferred candidate lost. records.title: Major losses could spur Trump to escalate war before year's end
records.summary: As much as the Iran war is the key reason Trump and the GOP were crushed tonight, it is important to recognize that the pressure for war is now likely to increase . This does not mean that Trump will restart the war. But the balance of pressure for and against war will likely favor escalation. Trump was under a degree of pressure to strike a deal before the midterms, hoping to soften the blow in the polls. But now that the midterms are over, that pressure will dissipate somewhat. Gas prices are still high, but the political cost has already been paid. There won’t be another point on the political calendar for some time when that cost can be exacted again. But two other factors will intensify. First, pro-war elements in Israel and in Washington will see the next two months as the last period in which Trump has wide maneuverability to restart the war. By January, the Democrats will control both chambers, will control the purse, and can begin impeaching Trump’s secretaries, including Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. records.title: Sanders, Slotkin say they won’t back Schumer for majority leader
records.summary: Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) announced Tuesday that they would not back Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) in his effort to become majority leader next year. The duo — leading voices on the center and left of the Democratic Party — took pains to avoid discussing specific policy issues, arguing instead that it is time for a new generation of leaders to take charge. "If this campaign was about anything, it was about change," Sanders said, adding that “poll after poll suggests that the American people want bold change.” “The public is done with people who say a lot of words but aren’t actually going to put more money in people’s pockets,” Slotkin said. “I personally will work with anyone who wants to work on that mission instead of looking like we’re doing things.” Neither Sanders nor Slotkin specified who they would support in the race for majority leader, though Slotkin said she had a “productive conversation” with Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Mary.) about his potential candidacy. The joint press conference suggests that momentum is building behind the effort to find new Democratic leadership in the Senate. records.summary: Unless you’ve been living under a rock (no shame Patrick Star!), you’ve likely heard about last Tuesday’s “Blue Wave” midterm elections . The Democrats’ strong performance at the polls flipped control of the House and the Senate, delivering stunning results on the way, including flipping long-time red states like Kansas and Texas. As the GOP scrambles to repair the damage and Democrats strategize about how to use their new power in a divided Washington, one takeaway seems obvious: this was a foreign policy election, in which the Iran war and the costs it brought home served as the tipping point. records.title: 'Junk history' and Swedish neutrality
records.summary: The historian Stephen Kotkin of Stanford’s Hoover Institution has penned an important new essay on the phenomenon of “junk history”: reductionist or plainly wrong interpretations of historical events that have little or no basis in empirical reality but are nevertheless “marshaled in policy debates as justification for action, up to launching wars.” The emblematic example, which has recently been used by advocates for the war with Iran, is the failure of British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain to truly ensure “peace in our time” at Munich in 1938. As Kotkin once put it, “It turns out not everything is Munich. It turns out Munich wasn’t even Munich when you get down into the nitty-gritty details.” Another example of junk history is what many otherwise well-informed American observers think they know about Sweden’s conduct during World War II and the Cold War. records.title: Scorned Trump boots Rwanda, South Africa from trade deal
records.summary: Last week, the Trump administration announced that, beginning January 1, South Africa and Rwanda will stop receiving preferential trade access to the U.S. market through the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA). This decision comes down to issues that have little to do with the act itself, nor even really with trade between the United States and these countries. Rather, in both cases, their removal from AGOA serves as an act of retribution from a president unhappy with their governments’ policies on domestic or regional issues. But American interests themselves will suffer, as consumers will be forced to pay higher prices for the same goods. The preferential trade agreement — originally signed into law in 2000 by President Bill Clinton and most recently renewed in September for two additional years — provides duty-free access for over 7,000 goods to the U.S. market for qualifying sub-Saharan countries. In exchange for this preferential access, AGOA requires countries to meet a set of vague requirements, including reducing barriers to American exporters, ensuring governance and human rights standards, and not posing a threat to U.S. national security and foreign policy interest

methodology.reliability: A official primary source/catalogue; B established newsroom or independent research; C specialist, advocacy or aggregator; D alternative commentary; E unverified social/community; U unclassified. Grade describes source class, not the truth of a specific claim.
methodology.confidence: Claim confidence is left unassessed unless an upstream collector supplies a numeric value. Source grade is not claim confidence.
methodology.corroboration: The six views reuse the existing archive. Similar stories, repeated posts, syndicated copy or multiple outlets quoting one origin are not independent corroboration. A human must inspect provenance.
methodology.geolocation: Location is shown only when supplied by the source or upstream archive. No location is inferred from a headline.
methodology.limits: This is open-source situational awareness, not intelligence agency coverage, an emergency warning service, a live market terminal or a verified threat assessment.
